title: 6 Best Marble Sealers in 2026: Stop Stains (Not Etching)
metaDescription: Tenax Proseal tops 6 marble sealers for most counters; Dry-Treat Stain-Proof Plus for heavy cooking. Plus why no sealer can stop etching on marble.
intro:
The best marble sealer for most countertops and vanities is Tenax Proseal, an impregnator that keeps water and oil stains out while leaving polished marble looking untouched. For a white marble island next to a busy cooktop, Dry-Treat Stain-Proof Plus offers even stronger oil resistance.

Before you buy anything, know what a sealer can and cannot do. It slows stains from coffee, wine and cooking oil. It does nothing to stop etching, the dull marks lemon juice and vinegar leave on marble, because that is a chemical reaction with the stone itself. This guide ranks six sealers, then covers etching, finishes, how to test your marble, which product suits counters, bathrooms, floors and outdoor stone, and how to apply it without haze.
quickAnswer: Use Tenax Proseal on most polished marble counters, Dry-Treat Stain-Proof Plus where oil stains are the big risk, StoneTech BulletProof in bathrooms and showers, and Miracle 511 when you need a store-shelf option today. Use Tenax Ager only on honed, tumbled or dark marble after a test patch. Seal for stains, and manage etching with coasters, quick wipe-ups and a polishing compound.

sections.heading: Best Marble Sealer: The Short Answer
sections.body:
| Pick | Best for | Key spec |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tenax Proseal | Polished marble counters | Water and oil impregnator, invisible |
| Dry-Treat Stain-Proof Plus | High-value white marble, heavy cooking | Fluorinated, breathable, interior and exterior |
| Miracle Sealants 511 | Buying today, mixed stone and grout | Solvent-carried impregnator |
| StoneTech BulletProof | Showers, bathroom floors, vanities | Water-based, low odor, seals grout too |
| Tenax Ager | Honed, tumbled or dark marble | Color-enhancing impregnator |
| Granite Gold Sealer | Top-ups between full sealings | Water-based trigger spray |

Every product on this list is an impregnator: it soaks into the stone and lines the pores instead of forming a coating. That is what you want on marble, because a surface film scratches, wears unevenly and can make polished stone look plastic.

Most marble disappointment comes from expecting a sealer to stop etching. It will not. A good one buys you minutes to hours to wipe up coffee, wine or oil before color soaks in, and that is the job to shop for.

sections.heading: The 6 Best Marble Sealers in 2026, Ranked
sections.body:
The ranking weighs each maker's technical data sheet, the stone types and finishes the label approves, the stated reapplication guidance and recurring owner feedback about stains after sealing. Products scored higher for strong oil repellency, no change to the look of polished marble and forgiving application. Nothing here comes from trials of our own.

### Best Overall: Tenax Proseal

Tenax supplies stone fabricators worldwide, and Proseal is its impregnator for calcite stones such as marble, limestone and travertine. It soaks into the stone and blocks both water-based and oil-based stains while leaving the surface looking exactly as it did, which matters on polished Carrara or Calacatta, where any haze or added gloss stands out under kitchen lights. Polished marble is fairly tight at the surface, so one careful coat often reaches the pores that matter, with a second pass on the thirstier zones around the sink. Apply to clean, dry stone, keep it wet through the dwell time on the label, then buff off every trace of excess. Owners commonly report wine and coffee wiping away cleanly on counters treated with it, while acids still etch, as they will under any sealer. It is mostly sold online and through stone suppliers rather than in hardware aisles.

**Pros:** strong water and oil repellency; invisible on polished marble; a little goes a long way; fabricator-grade.

**Cons:** harder to find locally; costs more per ounce than mainstream brands.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Tenax+Proseal+marble+sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Premium: Dry-Treat Stain-Proof Plus

Dry-Treat is an Australian brand with a long-standing reputation among stone restorers, and Stain-Proof Plus is its high-performance impregnator for dense and polished surfaces. It uses fluorinated chemistry, the class of sealer that resists oil best, and oil is what turns white marble a yellow-gray shadow beside a cooktop. The maker states that it lets the stone breathe, so moisture from below is not trapped, and rates it for interior and exterior stone. The price makes the most sense on large or valuable installations where a stain would be expensive to fix, such as a book-matched Calacatta island. Application follows the usual impregnator steps, but the label puts extra weight on letting it cure fully before the surface sees water, and that patience is part of getting the advertised result. Expect a long interval between applications compared with budget products, which offsets part of the cost.

**Pros:** top-tier oil and water repellency; interior and exterior rating; breathable; long service life claims.

**Cons:** expensive for a small vanity; demands careful wipe-off and the full cure time.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Dry-Treat+Stain-Proof+Plus&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Value Classic: Miracle Sealants 511 Impregnator

Miracle 511 has been on tile-shop shelves for decades, and it is the marble sealer you can most often buy today rather than order. A solvent carrier helps it travel into the stone, and the maker approves it for marble along with most other natural stone and cement grout. That versatility helps if you are sealing a marble vanity top and the tile floor around it on the same afternoon. It gives solid water repellency and moderate oil protection, which is enough for bathrooms, floors and lightly used kitchens. For a polished marble counter next to a busy cooktop, a fluoropolymer product such as Dry-Treat or Proseal holds off oil better. Ventilate well while you work; the smell is strong for a few hours, then fades. On polished marble, which shows residue more than speckled granite does, wipe and buff the excess with extra care before it tacks up.

**Pros:** easy to find; proven on marble, limestone and travertine; adds no sheen; fair price per quart.

**Cons:** strong solvent smell during application; less oil resistance than fluoropolymer sealers.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Miracle+Sealants+511+Impregnator&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Bathrooms: StoneTech BulletProof Sealer

BulletProof is a water-based penetrating sealer, and its low odor makes it the sensible choice for marble showers, bathroom floors and vanities, where ventilation is poor and solvent fumes would hang around. The maker rates it for interior and exterior natural stone, including marble and limestone, and for grout, so in a shower you can treat the stone and the grout lines in one pass. Honed marble absorbs more than polished, so plan on two applications on honed shower walls and floors, letting the first soak in before adding the second. Once cured, it does not change the color or finish of the stone. In a shower, keep the space dry for the full cure window on the label before anyone turns on the water. It costs a bit more than other water-based options, but in a small bathroom you are buying a single quart at most.

**Pros:** low odor for small rooms; rated for showers, floors and counters; seals stone and grout together; water cleanup.

**Cons:** honed marble may need two coats; pricier than other water-based sealers.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=StoneTech+BulletProof+Sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Color Enhancer: Tenax Ager

Tenax Ager is a color-enhancing impregnator: it seals while darkening the stone to a wet-look tone and making the veining stand out. On honed, brushed or tumbled marble, which often looks dusty and flat, the change can be striking in a good way, and on dark marbles such as Nero Marquina or Emperador it restores depth that a honed finish takes away. It is the wrong product for a polished white counter whose appeal is its brightness. On white stone, enhancers can look blotchy or yellowish, and the effect is not easy to undo. Always try it on a spare tile or a hidden patch and judge it fully dry the next day in daylight. Apply it thinly with a cloth and remove all excess, especially from honed surfaces, where residue shows as a sticky film. Exterior marble that has weathered pale is another good use.

**Pros:** deepens color and veining on honed or tumbled marble; seals at the same time; revives weathered stone.

**Cons:** permanent darkening; not for polished white marble; needs a test patch first.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Tenax+Ager+color+enhancer&tag=sktiger-20)

### Easiest Upkeep: Granite Gold Sealer

Despite the name, Granite Gold Sealer is labeled for marble and other natural stone as well as granite. It is a water-based trigger spray: mist clean, dry stone, let it sit briefly and wipe it dry. That makes it the simplest product here, and many owners keep a bottle under the sink for the busiest spots, such as the coffee station or the strip beside the range. As the main sealer on honed or porous marble it is outclassed by the impregnators above, which go deeper and last longer. The smart approach is a full sealing with Proseal, Dry-Treat or BulletProof, followed by a light pass of this spray every few months on the heaviest-use zones to keep repellency strong between full treatments. You can find it in big-box and grocery stores, which helps when you notice water darkening the stone and want to act the same day.

**Pros:** spray-and-wipe with no tools; widely sold; low odor; good for top-ups.

**Cons:** lighter protection than true impregnators; needs reapplying more often.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Granite+Gold+Sealer+spray&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.heading: Does Marble Sealer Stop Etching or Just Stains?
sections.body:
### Etching is chemical damage

Marble is mostly calcite, a form of calcium carbonate. Acids dissolve a microscopic layer of it, leaving a dull, slightly rough mark on polished stone. Citrus, vinegar, wine, tomato sauce, soda, many juices and acidic cleaners all etch. The mark is physical damage on the surface, not something absorbed, so it cannot be wiped off.

### Staining is absorption

A stain happens when a liquid enters the pores and leaves color behind. Oil darkens marble, coffee and tea leave brown marks and red wine leaves pink to purple ones. This is exactly what a sealer slows down.

### Why red wine does both

Red wine is acidic and pigmented, so on marble it can etch and stain at once. A sealer handles the color, but the acid still dulls the surface. That is why a sealed counter can show a dull ring where a glass sat overnight, and why owners sometimes conclude their sealer failed when it did the part it can do.

### What to do about it

Treat the two problems separately. Use a quality impregnator for stains. For etching, use coasters, trivets and cutting boards, blot acidic spills right away, and keep a marble polishing compound for light etches on polished surfaces. Fix etches first, then seal, because polishing removes the sealer along with the damaged layer.

sections.heading: Does Your Marble Need Sealing? How to Test It
sections.body:
### The water test

Put a few drops of water on several spots, including next to the sink and cooktop. If the marble darkens under the water within about five minutes, it needs sealing now. If it takes 15 to 30 minutes, sealing is still worthwhile, especially in a kitchen. If nothing changes after half an hour, the current seal or the stone itself is holding well.

### The oil test

Place a few drops of cooking oil on a hidden spot, such as a sink-cutout offcut or under an overhang. Wait 10 to 15 minutes and wipe. A dark shadow left behind means oil is getting in. Oil stains are the hardest to lift from marble, so if this test fails, an oil-repelling product such as Dry-Treat or Proseal is the better buy.

### Skip the lemon test

Lemon juice will etch marble whether it is sealed or not, so it tells you nothing except that the stone contains calcite, which you already know.

### New installations

Test a week or so after the stone goes in. Fabricators do not always seal, and some use a light shop product that wears off quickly. Testing yourself tells you where you actually stand, rather than relying on what the installer remembers.

sections.heading: What Is the Best Sealer for Polished, Honed or Tumbled Marble?
sections.body:
### Polished

Polished marble is ground to a glassy shine and is relatively tight at the surface, which helps it resist stains, but etches stand out dramatically against the gloss. One coat of an invisible impregnator, sometimes two near the sink, is usually enough. Proseal and Dry-Treat are the top choices because neither adds sheen or haze.

### Honed

Honed marble is ground smooth without the final polish. It absorbs more than polished, so it stains more readily and usually needs two coats. Etches blend into the matte surface, which is why many designers recommend honed marble for kitchens.

### Leathered or brushed

These textured finishes hide etching best but absorb unevenly. Apply sealer with a soft brush to reach into the texture and wipe the excess so it does not pool in low spots.

### Tumbled

Tumbled tile, common on backsplashes and rustic floors, is the most porous and usually takes two or three coats. It is also the best candidate for an enhancer like Tenax Ager if you want richer color.

| Finish | Stain risk | Etch visibility | Coats |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Polished | Lower | High | 1, sometimes 2 |
| Honed | Higher | Low | 2 |
| Leathered / brushed | Higher | Very low | 2, brushed in |
| Tumbled | Highest | Very low | 2 to 3 |

### Color enhancer on white marble?

Be careful. Enhancers darken stone permanently, and on white Carrara or Calacatta the result can look blotchy or yellowish. Test on a spare tile first and judge it the next day in daylight.

sections.heading: Which Marble Sealer Is Best for Countertops, Bathrooms, Floors and Outdoors?
sections.body:
### Kitchen countertops

Choose an impregnator with strong oil repellency and no effect on sheen: Tenax Proseal or Dry-Treat Stain-Proof Plus. A kitchen is where oil rings happen, and one dark shadow near the stove costs more to remove than the sealer costs to buy. If your kitchen mixes marble and granite, our [granite sealer guide](/best-granite-sealer/) covers which products handle both.

### Bathrooms and showers

Use a water-based, low-odor sealer such as StoneTech BulletProof. Small rooms trap solvent fumes, and the stain risks are cosmetics, soap scum and hair dye rather than cooking oil. Seal stone and grout together so you track one product and one schedule. Keep mildew in check with a stone-safe cleaner; harsh mildew sprays strip sealer, so read our [mold remover guide](/best-mold-remover/) for gentler options.

### Floors and tile

The main threats are grit, water and the odd spill. A mid-priced impregnator such as Miracle 511 or BulletProof is enough. Plan two coats on honed tile, buy by the gallon for big areas and put walk-off mats at every entry, because grit scratches marble faster than anything else.

### Exterior marble

Outdoors, acid rain slowly etches marble and freeze-thaw stresses it. Use a breathable impregnator rated for exterior use, such as Dry-Treat, and accept a soft patina over time. Marble pavers set in sand behave like other paver systems; our [paver sealer guide](/best-paver-sealer/) covers joint sand and breathable products.

sections.heading: Is There a Permanent Sealer for Marble? What About Engineered Marble?
sections.body:
### Permanent sealers

Products marketed as permanent marble sealers are usually professionally applied surface coatings or treatments, not the impregnators on this list. Some claim etch resistance as well as stain resistance, but a coating changes how the stone looks and feels, and if it scratches or wears through, repair is a professional job. Before you buy one, ask the applicator what happens when the surface is scratched, how a damaged area is repaired and what the written warranty covers. For most homes, a good impregnator renewed every one to three years is cheaper and easier to live with.

### Engineered marble

Engineered marble is crushed stone bound with resin, made to look like marble. Most of it is far less absorbent than natural stone, and many makers say it needs no sealer. Follow the manufacturer's care sheet, and if a sealer is allowed, use one approved for engineered stone rather than a natural-stone impregnator that will just sit on top as haze.

### Cultured marble

Cultured marble, common on one-piece vanity tops, is a cast product with a gel coat on top. It is not porous, does not need stone sealer and will not accept it. Clean it with non-abrasive cleaners and treat dull spots or chips as gel-coat repairs.

### Marble slabs and tables

A marble table top or loose slab is sealed the same way as a counter. Seal the top and edges, and give the edges an extra pass, since cut edges absorb more than the polished face.

sections.heading: How Do You Apply Marble Sealer Without Haze?
sections.body:
### Clean and dry first

Wash the stone with a pH-neutral stone cleaner and poultice out any stains before sealing, because sealer locks in whatever is already in the pores. Let the marble dry at least 24 hours after cleaning, or 48 after a poultice. Mask nearby wood and paint with painter's tape.

### Apply and dwell

Spread sealer evenly with a lint-free cloth, foam pad or soft brush over a few square feet at a time. Keep the surface wet for the dwell time on the label, typically 5 to 15 minutes, and add product where it disappears fast; those are the most absorbent spots.

### Wipe off every drop

Before it starts to tack up, wipe off all excess with clean, dry cloths and buff until the stone looks exactly as it did before. Polished marble shows residue more than any other stone. If the label calls for a second coat, apply it within the stated window, then wipe again.

### Let it cure

Keep water, cleaners and food off the surface for the full cure, usually 24 to 72 hours. If haze shows the next day, rub a little of the same sealer on the spot to re-dissolve the residue, then buff dry immediately. Do not scrub haze with abrasive pads, which will dull the polish.

sections.heading: How Often Should You Seal Marble, and What Does It Cost?
sections.body:
### How often

Run the water test every six to twelve months. When water darkens the stone within about five minutes, reseal. Busy kitchen counters typically need it every one to two years, and bathroom vanities and floors often go two to three. Premium fluorinated sealers usually last longer between coats than budget products on the same stone. Write the date inside a cabinet door so you are not guessing.

### Daily care that protects the seal

Clean with a stone-safe neutral cleaner or a few drops of dish soap in warm water. Vinegar, lemon, glass cleaner, bleach and many all-purpose sprays either etch marble directly or break the sealer down. Blot spills rather than smearing them, since smearing spreads acid over a wider area.

### Quantity and DIY cost

A kitchen with 40 to 50 square feet of counter needs well under a quart, even for two coats on honed stone. A 100-square-foot bathroom floor may need one to two quarts depending on porosity. Doing it yourself, the cost is one bottle and some cloths.

### Professional sealing and repair

Stone-care companies commonly quote roughly $150 to $400 to seal a kitchen, more when polishing or stain removal is added. Deep etches that feel rough need honing and polishing by a pro. For routine resealing, DIY gives the same result, because the chemistry is the same.

mistakes.title: Expecting sealer to stop etching
mistakes.body: Every marble sealer targets stains, not acid reactions. If you expect a sealed counter to shrug off lemon juice, you will end up reapplying a sealer that was already working. Manage etching with coasters, quick cleanup and polishing compound instead.

mistakes.title: Using an enhancer on white marble without testing
mistakes.body: Color enhancers darken stone permanently, and on white Carrara or Calacatta the result can look blotchy or yellow. Try the product on a spare tile or hidden spot, let it dry overnight and check it in daylight before treating the whole surface.

mistakes.title: Leaving sealer to dry on the surface
mistakes.body: Polished marble shows every bit of residue as a cloudy smear. Wipe and buff thoroughly within the time on the label. If haze shows up later, reactivate it with a little fresh sealer on a cloth and buff it off rather than scrubbing.

mistakes.title: Cleaning with vinegar or citrus sprays
mistakes.body: Natural cleaning recipes rely on vinegar or lemon, and both etch marble on contact. Many all-purpose sprays are acidic or strongly alkaline and strip the sealer over time. Use a cleaner labeled pH-neutral and safe for natural stone.

mistakes.title: Sealing over existing stains
mistakes.body: Sealer traps whatever is already in the stone. Poultice out coffee rings or oil shadows first, let the marble dry a day or two, then seal. Sealing over a stain makes it permanent and makes later poultice attempts much less effective.

faqs.q: What is the best marble sealer?
faqs.a: Tenax Proseal is the best marble sealer for most polished counters and vanities because it repels water and oil without changing the look of the stone. Dry-Treat Stain-Proof Plus is the premium choice for white marble near a cooktop, and StoneTech BulletProof is the best low-odor option for bathrooms and showers.

faqs.q: What is the best sealer for marble countertops?
faqs.a: An impregnating sealer with strong oil repellency, such as Tenax Proseal or Dry-Treat Stain-Proof Plus. Kitchens see olive oil, butter and wine, and oil stains are the hardest to remove from marble. Avoid topical coatings made for concrete, which scratch and peel on a counter and make the stone look plastic.

faqs.q: Can any marble sealer make marble etch-proof?
faqs.a: No impregnating sealer stops etching, because etching is a chemical reaction between acid and the calcite in the stone. Some professionally applied surface coatings claim etch resistance, but they change the look and feel of the marble and need professional repair if damaged. For most homes, habits and polishing compound are the answer.

faqs.q: What is the best marble sealer for a bathroom?
faqs.a: StoneTech BulletProof is the best fit for most marble bathrooms. It is water-based and low odor, which matters in small rooms with weak ventilation, and it is rated for showers, floors, vanities and grout. Plan two coats on honed marble and keep the shower dry through the full cure time on the label.

faqs.q: How often should marble be sealed?
faqs.a: Test with water every six to twelve months and reseal when the stone darkens within about five minutes. Busy kitchen counters typically need resealing every one to two years, while bathroom vanities and floors often go two to three years. Premium fluorinated sealers usually last longer between coats than budget products.

faqs.q: Does engineered marble need a sealer?
faqs.a: Usually not. Engineered marble is crushed stone bound with resin and is far less absorbent than natural marble, so many makers say it needs no sealer. Follow the manufacturer care sheet. Cultured marble vanity tops have a gel coat and should never be treated with a natural stone sealer.

faqs.q: Why is my marble hazy after sealing?
faqs.a: Haze is excess sealer that dried on the surface. Put a small amount of the same sealer on a clean cloth, rub the hazy area for a minute to re-dissolve the residue, then buff completely dry. For stubborn haze, the sealer maker usually names a solvent that removes it. Avoid abrasive pads on polished marble.

bottomLine: For most marble counters, Tenax Proseal gives the best balance of stain protection, invisibility and value. For high-value white marble near a cooktop, Dry-Treat Stain-Proof Plus earns its premium; for bathrooms and showers, StoneTech BulletProof does the job without solvent fumes; and Miracle 511 is the reliable shelf option. Seal for stains, and manage etching with habits: coasters, cutting boards, a neutral cleaner and a jar of polishing compound will do more for how your marble looks in five years than any bottle on this list.
